column1: # These are ceilings, not benchmarks. They exist to catch a snippet that
# regressed into doing real work (an accidental O(n^2) loop, a sleep, a
# runaway allocation), not to rank the four languages against each other.
# Every snippet here prints under twenty lines and allocates almost nothing,
# so what the numbers actually measure is runtime startup:
#   rust    ~2ms    ~1.5MB   static binary, no runtime to start
#   go      ~3ms    ~4MB     goroutine scheduler and GC come up first
#   python  ~19ms   ~15MB    interpreter start plus stdlib import
#   node    ~50ms   ~70MB    V8 heap reservation dominates everything
# (Measured on an M-series laptop. CI runners are slower, which is why the
# ceilings below are roughly five times the observed time and two to four
# times the observed memory, since RSS varies with libc and kernel.)
# Ceilings are uniform within a language on purpose: the spread between
# snippets in the same language is measurement noise, so a per-snippet number
# would imply a precision that is not there. A row that genuinely needs a
# different ceiling should say why in a comment above it.
# Wall time is the minimum of LR_BENCH_RUNS runs (default 5); memory is the
# peak RSS across them. See bin/measure.py for why those two statistics.
